content: In optics, a virtual image is an image formed when the outgoing light rays from a point on an object do not actually converge at a single point. A common example of this is the image seen in a flat mirror. When you look at yourself in a flat mirror, the image appears to be located at a distance behind the mirror equal to the distance you are standing in front of it. For instance, if you are standing 0.5 meters in front of the mirror, your image will appear to be 0.5 meters behind the mirror. In contrast, a real image is formed when the outgoing light rays from a point on an object converge at a single point. Real images can be observed most easily when they are projected onto an opaque screen. However, the presence of a screen is not a requirement for the formation of a real image. For example, when you look through a diverging lens (a lens with at least one concave surface) or into a convex mirror, the image you see is a virtual image. On the other hand, when you observe a focused image on a screen placed behind a converging lens (a lens with at least one convex surface) or in front of a concave mirror, the image is a real image because the light rays actually converge at the location of the screen. If you position yourself so that the screen is directly between you and the optical device (such as a mirror or lens), you can remove the screen and still observe the real image because the light rays are physically converging at that point. It is also worth noting that converging lenses and concave mirrors can produce virtual images if the object is located within the focal length of the optical device. For example, a plane mirror or a convex mirror always forms a virtual image that appears to be located behind the mirror. Although the light rays seem to originate from behind the mirror, the actual light rays only exist and spread out in front of the mirror. In optical system diagrams, virtual rays are typically represented by dotted lines. These virtual rays indicate the perceived paths of light as seen by an observer looking into the optical device. However, it is important to understand that these dotted lines do not represent the actual paths of light. The actual light rays, which are represented by solid lines, indicate the true paths along which light travels. A point on the virtual image is located where the virtual rays, as perceived by the observer, appear to intersect.
